doc.title: Anne Phillips interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2025

title: Her album Born to Be Blue and its rediscovery
summary: Through Joe Reisman at Roulette she recorded her first album at 23, later rediscovered by an engineer and reissued on CD.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: But the best thing that happened on something that wasn’t one of those, I was at Dick Charles’ studio. And he called me up and said, “I think there’s an elderly man who’s written a lot of music for the Kraft Music Hall themes and stuff, Vladimir Solinsky. And © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

he has some songs he’s had lyrics put to and I think you’re the right singer to do it. And so I did and they were beautiful but not hip type songs. They were beautiful songs. And about two months later I got a call from the studio and they said, “Call Joe Reisman over at Roulette Records, he wants to talk to you.” And that’s where my album, the first one, “Born to be Blue” came, because he had an idea or he had a song that he wanted to use as the title song. Actually that was “Lonelyville.” And we did the whole recording and he called the most wonderful arranger, Kermit Levinsky. And there I was, 23 years old and brand new in the business, and Milt Hinton, Osie Johnson, Dick Hyman, full string section, Doc Severinsen on trumpet. And so I did that album, which is quite beautiful and it got great reviews and you know, “Watch this singer there’s no comparison” and all that good stuff in Billboard. And then of course it was ’59, ’60 — rock was coming in — so there wasn’t any second album. But, and this is the amazing thing that happened, about 15 years later I was doing some record dates back up in Bell South, and this young engineer caught me in the hallway and said, “Anne, I was doing inventory here and I found something you might like to have. Don’t ever tell anybody who gave this to you.” And he gave me a 7-1/2 copy of the record which is now “Born to be Blue.” They discovered that somebody had used “Lonelyville” as a title song so they flipped it and so the B side became the A side and the first tune on that was “Born to be Blue.” And that’s as the years went on I found out that it was known all over, they had released it in Japan and never told me, but all over the world people knew it. And I was finally doing another album — I don’t think you still call them albums anymore. And the promoter I got, Virginia Wicks, who you may have heard of. I sent “Born to be Blue” to her and said, “This is something I did years ago.” And she said, “Oh my God I would love to promote that.” And I said, “ Well I’m on it.” She said, “Who cares?” So it was pressed on a CD and it got great reviews, I mean just incredible reviews. And more people knew about it and bought it. And nobody ever knew.
